# OpenStreetMap data {#sec-m4-osm}

OSM is the most complete and up-to-date road dataset freely available in Brazil, and it is the
input of any routing. There are two access routes, for different needs.

```{r}
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# default basemap for mapview(): OpenStreetMap
mapview::mapviewOptions(basemaps = c("OpenStreetMap", "Esri.WorldGrayCanvas", "Esri.WorldImagery"))
```

| Package | How it works | When to use it |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `osmdata` | queries the Overpass API live | small areas, specific features, rare attributes |
| `osmextract` | downloads ready-made regional `.pbf` extracts (Geofabrik) | a whole road network, input for `r5r` |

The rule of thumb: if the answer fits in a few thousand features, `osmdata`; if you want
"all the roads in a state", `osmextract`.

::: {.callout-important}
## Before you start: the module data

Run the module's setup script once. It installs the missing packages, downloads the
module's data package (`dados_modulo4.zip`, from the
[Releases](https://github.com/Joaobazzo/curso-r-transportes/releases) page) to `dados/brutos/` and
checks whether R can see Java 21, which `r5r` requires:

```{r}
#| eval: false
source("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Joaobazzo/curso-r-transportes/main/R/preparar_modulo4.R")
```

The package has the São Paulo–Santos network used in this chapter and in @sec-m4-roteamento, Ipea's
results for Fortaleza (`aopdata`) and the `dados/brutos/fortaleza/` folder, with the OSM network
and the GTFS that `r5r` uses in @sec-m4-r5r. The script ends with the message **Tudo pronto
para o Módulo 4** ("All set for Module 4").

**If the download is blocked by the server.** On restricted networks, such as the Ministry's, the
server may refuse downloads made by R. The message usually contains `HTTP 403`, `Forbidden`,
`cannot open URL` or "Não foi possível baixar os dados do módulo" ("could not download the module data"). In that case, do it by hand:

1. In the browser, download
   [`dados_modulo4.zip`](https://github.com/Joaobazzo/curso-r-transportes/releases/download/dados-modulo4/dados_modulo4.zip)
   (about 70 MB).
2. Unzip the file **inside the project folder**, the one with the
   `curso-r-transportes.Rproj` file. The files go to `dados/brutos/`.
3. Run the `source()` again. It finds the data, skips the download and checks the rest.

If the `source()` itself fails, download the script
[`preparar_modulo4.R`](https://github.com/Joaobazzo/curso-r-transportes/blob/main/R/preparar_modulo4.R)
in the browser (download button in the top-right corner), save it in the project folder and run
`source("preparar_modulo4.R")`.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## In Brazil, use OSM for the road network, and almost only for that

The **road network** is the best-mapped OSM layer in Brazil: the coverage of streets and
highways is broad, the geometry is good and the connectivity is what routing engines
expect. That is what this module uses OSM for: as the input for routing with `dodgr`
(@sec-m4-roteamento) and `r5r` (@sec-m4-gtfs).

The **other features** are a different story. Ports, terminals, aerodromes, bridges, weight and height
restrictions, land use and points of interest depend on who mapped each place: the
coverage is uneven, the attributes are partial and the classification changes from one city to
another. The examples with ports and bridges in this chapter show exactly that. For these
layers, prefer the official sources:

| What you need | Most suitable source |
|:--|:--|
| Federal highways, with code, segment and status | SNV, from DNIT |
| Port facilities | ANTAQ |
| Railways, waterways and terminals | geospatial datasets of the Ministry of Transport and Infra S.A. (ONTL) |
| Aerodromes | ANAC |
| Continuous base map (roads, hydrography, localities) | IBGE, BC250 |
| Addresses and establishments | IBGE, CNEFE (it is what `geocodebr` uses, @sec-m3-geocodificacao) |
| General catalogue of official geospatial data | INDE |

OSM is still useful for these layers as a **quick check** or when there is no official
source, but in that case the report must say that the data are collaborative and incomplete.
:::

## `osmdata`: Overpass queries

Every query has the same structure: an area (`opq`), one or more tag filters
(`add_osm_feature`) and the output format (`osmdata_sf`).

```{r}
arquivo <- "dados/brutos/portos_osm.gpkg"

if (!file.exists(arquivo)) {
  res <- osmdata::opq(bbox = c(-48.75, -25.65, -48.35, -25.35), timeout = 120) |>
    osmdata::add_osm_feature(key = "seamark:type", value = "harbour") |>
    osmdata::osmdata_sf()

  res$osm_points |>
    filter(!is.na(`seamark:type`)) |>     # discards the nodes that only draw other features
    select(any_of(c("osm_id", "name", "seamark:harbour:category"))) |>
    st_write(arquivo, quiet = TRUE)
}

portos_osm <- st_read(arquivo, quiet = TRUE)
nrow(portos_osm)
```

The query asks for the points marked as a harbour on the nautical chart (`seamark:type = harbour`) in
Paranaguá Bay. A quick check on the map:

```{r}
mapview::mapview(portos_osm, col.regions = "#1a5b8a", layer.name = "Ports and marinas (OSM)")
```

Look at what came back: terminals, yacht clubs and marinas mixed together. In OSM, a "harbour" is what the
mapper decided to call a harbour. For the official list of port facilities, the source is
ANTAQ.

The object returned by `osmdata_sf()` has several components, because a single query can
return different types of geometry:

```{r}
#| eval: false
res$osm_points        # nodes
res$osm_lines         # open ways
res$osm_polygons      # closed ways (areas)
res$osm_multilines    # line relations (a whole highway, for example)
res$osm_multipolygons # area relations (municipalities, areas with holes)
```

### The tags that matter in transport

```{r}
#| eval: false
# road hierarchy
add_osm_feature(key = "highway", value = c("motorway", "trunk", "primary"))

# a specific highway by its code
add_osm_feature(key = "ref", value = "BR-116")
```

`osmdata::available_tags("highway")` lists every possible value of a key — useful
because OSM's taxonomy is extensive and it is worth checking before assuming.

```{r}
osmdata::available_tags("highway") |> head(12)
```

### A complete example: bridges and restrictions in a corridor

```{r}
arquivo_pontes <- "dados/brutos/pontes_br116.gpkg"

if (!file.exists(arquivo_pontes)) {
  res <- osmdata::opq(bbox = c(-49.40, -25.75, -48.40, -25.15), timeout = 180) |>
    osmdata::add_osm_feature(key = "bridge", value = "yes") |>
    osmdata::osmdata_sf()

  pontes <- res$osm_lines |>
    filter(!is.na(highway)) |>
    select(any_of(c("osm_id", "name", "highway", "maxweight", "maxheight", "layer")))

  st_write(pontes, arquivo_pontes, quiet = TRUE)
}

pontes <- st_read(arquivo_pontes, quiet = TRUE)

c(pontes = nrow(pontes),
  com_restricao_peso = sum(!is.na(pontes$maxweight)))
```

This result often surprises people: most bridges **do not have** the weight restriction
mapped. It is the concrete illustration of OSM's limit — the geometry is good, the attribute is partial.
For official restrictions, the source is DNIT.

A quick look at the map confirms both points. First, where the bridges are, coloured
by road type:

```{r}
mapview::mapview(pontes, zcol = "highway", lwd = 3, layer.name = "Road type")
```

Then, only those with a mapped weight restriction. They are all on the Estrada da Graciosa: a sign
that someone mapped that road carefully, not that the other bridges have no limit.

```{r}
pontes_com_peso <- pontes |> filter(!is.na(maxweight))

mapview::mapview(pontes_com_peso, zcol = "maxweight", lwd = 4,
                 layer.name = "Maximum weight (t)")
```

## `osmextract`: the whole road network

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(osmextract)

# 1. find out which extract covers the area
oe_match("Ceará")
oe_match("Paraná")

# 2. download only the .pbf file (it is what r5r consumes, @sec-m4-gtfs)
oe_download(
  file_url = oe_match("Ceará")$url,
  download_directory = "dados/brutos/osm"
)

# 3. or read it straight as sf, filtering at the source with SQL
rede <- oe_get(
  place = "Ceará",
  layer = "lines",
  query = "SELECT osm_id, highway, name, maxspeed, oneway
           FROM lines
           WHERE highway IN ('motorway','trunk','primary','secondary','tertiary')",
  download_directory = "dados/brutos/osm"
)
```

The `query` argument is what makes this feasible: the filter runs on the file, and only the main
network reaches R. Without it, "all the lines in Ceará" are millions of features, most of them
irrelevant for routing.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Typical sizes

| Area | `.pbf` |
|:--|--:|
| A medium-sized city | 10–40 MB |
| A state | 50–600 MB |
| The whole of Brazil | > 2 GB |

Download the smallest extract that covers the study area. For a city, the metropolitan region is
enough; for interstate freight routing, the state. The `.pbf` of the whole of Brazil is rarely
needed — and it makes `r5r` very slow to build the network.
:::

## Preparing the network for routing

A raw road network download is not yet a navigable network. To follow the steps without
downloading a whole state's extract, we will use the country's main freight corridor: the
main roads between the city of **São Paulo and the Port of Santos**, with the two highways that
descend the escarpment, the Anchieta and the Imigrantes. The columns are the same as in `oe_get()` above.

The file comes in the module's data package (@sec-m3). The block below only downloads from OSM if it
is not in `dados/brutos/`, and that download is slow: the São Paulo network is large, and the
Overpass server may take several minutes or refuse the query (error 504).

```{r}
arquivo_rede <- "dados/brutos/rede_sao_paulo_santos.gpkg"

if (!file.exists(arquivo_rede)) {
  # Overpass mirror server, less congested than the main one
  osmdata::set_overpass_url("https://overpass.kumi.systems/api/interpreter")

  res <- osmdata::opq(bbox = c(-46.80, -24.02, -46.25, -23.45), timeout = 300) |>
    osmdata::add_osm_feature(key = "highway", value = c(
      "motorway", "motorway_link", "trunk", "trunk_link", "primary", "primary_link",
      "secondary", "secondary_link")) |>
    osmdata::osmdata_sf()

  res$osm_lines |>
    select(any_of(c("osm_id", "name", "ref", "highway", "maxspeed", "oneway", "lanes"))) |>
    st_write(arquivo_rede, quiet = TRUE)
}

rede <- st_read(arquivo_rede, quiet = TRUE) |>
  rename(geometry = geom)     # the GeoPackage calls the geometry "geom"
```

Three precautions:

```{r}
rede_limpa <- rede |>
  filter(!is.na(highway)) |>
  filter(!highway %in% c("footway", "path", "cycleway", "steps", "pedestrian")) |>
  mutate(
    velocidade = readr::parse_number(maxspeed),
    velocidade = dplyr::coalesce(velocidade, dplyr::case_match(
      highway,
      "motorway"  ~ 110,
      "trunk"     ~ 90,
      "primary"   ~ 80,
      "secondary" ~ 60,
      .default    = 40
    )),
    comprimento_m = as.numeric(st_length(geometry)),
    tempo_min = comprimento_m / 1000 / velocidade * 60
  )
```

The three points: (1) remove what cannot be travelled by the mode of interest; (2) fill in the
speed (`velocidade`) when the attribute is missing — and document the rule used; (3) compute the cost that the
routing will minimise (time, distance, or generalised cost).

Check the table: the first rows show whether the speed was filled in and whether each segment's
time (`tempo_min`) makes sense.

```{r}
rede_limpa |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(name, highway, maxspeed, velocidade, comprimento_m, tempo_min) |>
  head(10)
```

And check the map: the colour shows the speed assigned to each segment, mapped or filled in
by the rule. There are `r format(nrow(rede_limpa), big.mark = ",")` segments, too heavy for an
interactive map; to check it, the highways are enough, the `motorway` and `trunk` roads (on your
computer, `leafgl` from @sec-m2-sf can handle the whole network).

```{r}
# for display only (the calculations use the full network): merging the segments of the same
# highway with the same speed makes the map light without changing the drawing
rede_principal <- rede_limpa |>
  filter(highway %in% c("motorway", "trunk")) |>
  group_by(ref, velocidade) |>
  summarise(trechos = n(), .groups = "drop")

nrow(rede_principal)

mapview::mapview(rede_principal, zcol = "velocidade", layer.name = "Speed (km/h)")
```

## Geometric network × topological network

The clean network is still a **geometric network**: a collection of lines, each with its own
coordinates. It is good for drawing and measuring, but not for routing. To the computer, two
streets that cross on screen are not connected: nothing in the table says you can leave one and
enter the other.

Routing requires a **topological network**, or graph: a set of **nodes** (intersections, road
ends) and **edges** (the segments between two nodes), in which being connected means
**sharing a node**. The geometry becomes an attribute of the edge; what matters is who connects to
whom.

### A toy example

Three roads, drawn by hand:

- **Rua A** (horizontal) and **Rua B** (vertical) cross **at grade**: both have a
  vertex at the crossing point;
- **Viaduto C** (an overpass) goes over Rua A: the lines cross in the drawing, but there is no shared
  vertex, and there must be no connection.

```{r}
library(sfnetworks)

ruas <- st_sf(
  nome = c("Rua A", "Rua B", "Viaduto C"),
  geometry = st_sfc(
    st_linestring(rbind(c(0, 1), c(1, 1), c(2, 1))),    # vertex in the middle, at (1, 1)
    st_linestring(rbind(c(1, 0), c(1, 1), c(1, 2))),    # same vertex (1, 1)
    st_linestring(rbind(c(0.2, 0), c(0.6, 2)))          # crosses A at (0.4, 1), no vertex
  )
)
ruas
```

The most direct conversion, `as_sfnetwork()`, creates a node at each **end** of a line and one edge
per line:

```{r}
rede_ingenua <- as_sfnetwork(ruas, directed = FALSE)
rede_ingenua
```

There are 6 nodes and 3 edges, and the summary already warns: a "forest with 3 trees", that is, three
loose pieces. The crossing of roads A and B **did not become a node**, because the vertex (1, 1) is in the
middle of both lines, not at an end. That is exactly what happens with OSM: a way usually
crosses several intersections without being cut at them.

The fix is to **subdivide** the lines at the vertices they share:

```{r}
rede_topologica <- tidygraph::convert(rede_ingenua, to_spatial_subdivision)
rede_topologica
```

Now there are 7 nodes and 5 edges: the crossing (1, 1) became a node, and A and B were each cut into two
segments. The overpass stays separate, as it should, because it shares no vertex with
anyone. The three versions side by side:

```{r}
#| label: fig-rede-topologica
#| fig-cap: "The same network as geometry (left), as a naive graph (centre) and as a subdivided graph (right). The points are the nodes."
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-width: 9
desenhar_rede <- function(rede, titulo) {
  nos     <- st_as_sf(rede, "nodes")
  arestas <- st_as_sf(rede, "edges")

  ggplot() +
    geom_sf(data = arestas, aes(colour = nome), linewidth = 1.2) +
    geom_sf(data = nos, size = 2.5) +
    geom_sf_text(data = nos, aes(label = seq_len(nrow(nos))),
                 nudge_x = 0.12, nudge_y = 0.12, size = 3) +
    labs(title = titulo,
         subtitle = paste(nrow(nos), "nodes,", nrow(arestas), "edges"),
         colour = NULL) +
    theme_void(base_size = 9) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
}

geometrica <- ggplot(ruas) +
  geom_sf(aes(colour = nome), linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(title = "Geometric network", subtitle = "lines only, no connections", colour = NULL) +
  theme_void(base_size = 9) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

patchwork::wrap_plots(
  geometrica,
  desenhar_rede(rede_ingenua, "Naive graph"),
  desenhar_rede(rede_topologica, "Subdivided graph"),
  nrow = 1, guides = "collect"
) & theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The proof that the topology changed the result: ask for a path from the left end of Rua A to
the top end of Rua B.

```{r}
# in the naive graph: node 1 = (0, 1), node 4 = (1, 2). There is no path.
st_network_paths(rede_ingenua, from = 1, to = 4)$node_paths

# in the subdivided graph: node 1 = (0, 1), node 5 = (1, 2). The path goes through the crossing, node 2.
st_network_paths(rede_topologica, from = 1, to = 5)$node_paths
```

### What this means on the real network

`dodgr` and `r5r` do this conversion on their own, from OSM's own node
identifiers, which already mark where roads cross. But the logic is the same, and the same
problems show up:

- **Roads that should connect and do not**, because the mapper did not put in the shared node.
  The graph is split into isolated **components**, and a pair of points in different
  components "cannot reach each other". In the next chapter, the São Paulo–Santos corridor network
  becomes a graph with a few dozen components, and only the largest of them is fit for routing.
- **Roads that should not connect and do**, such as an overpass mapped with a node in common
  with the street below. The router then "comes down" from the overpass where there is no access. In OSM, the
  `layer` tag exists to prevent this.
- **Direction of travel**: in a directed graph (`directed = TRUE`), a one-way road
  becomes a single edge, and a two-way road becomes two, one in each direction. OSM's `oneway`
  tag is what defines this.

For a whole network with `sfnetworks`, the code is the same as in the example, applied to
`rede_limpa`:

```{r}
#| eval: false
net <- as_sfnetwork(rede_limpa, directed = FALSE) |>
  tidygraph::convert(sfnetworks::to_spatial_subdivision) |>
  tidygraph::activate("edges") |>
  mutate(peso = comprimento_m)
```

Now we have the two inputs of any routing: the origin and destination points, with
checked coordinates (@sec-m3-geocodificacao), and the road network, clean and ready to become a
graph. The next chapter links one to the other: it computes car distances, times and paths
on the São Paulo–Santos network.
